cervelt.origin: Cervelt is a trade name associated in this atlas with the downy undercoat of farmed red deer, Cervus elaphus, in New Zealand. The ownership, current producers and volumes behind the name could not be verified from primary sources. What is documented is the biology: red deer grow a winter coat of coarse guard hairs and fine underhairs, and the underhair was characterized in detail in 2010 by researchers at AgResearch in Lincoln, New Zealand.
cervelt.structure: Transmission and scanning electron microscopy of red deer winter coat show that all fiber types have overlapping cuticle cells around a cortex, often with a central medulla, but differ in diameter, cuticle thickness, scale pattern and the proportion of medulla. Fine underhairs resemble fine sheep wool: their intermediate filaments are arranged as in wool orthocortex and paracortex cells, with a similar bilateral distribution of the two cell types. Guard hairs and antler velvet hairs are more variable and resemble the heterotype cortex cells described in human hair.
cervelt.process: Red deer grow their winter coat under photoperiodic control: longer nightly melatonin secretion as days shorten depresses prolactin, and earlier onset of winter coat growth is associated with lower prolactin. In a British trial, melatonin implants advanced winter coat growth by 35 days, while lactation combined with restricted food delayed it by 20 days. Harvest would need to coincide with the molt of the winter coat and be followed by dehairing, scouring and spinning; the producer's actual collection and processing steps for Cervelt could not be verified.
cervelt.performance: No independent test data for Cervelt fabrics were found. Because the fine underhair has a wool-like bilateral cortex, it would be expected to behave like fine wool or cashmere in moisture uptake, flame behavior (charring and self-extinguishing) and acid dyeing, and to share their susceptibility to pilling, felting and attack by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae. Any claim of greater warmth or softness than cashmere is a producer claim to be checked against test reports.
cervelt.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior only. Deer guard hairs are recognizable microscopically by their scale pattern and prominent medulla, but fine underhair looks wool-like, so microscopy alone may not confirm deer origin in a blend. DNA or peptide mass spectrometry against authenticated red deer reference fiber would be needed to verify a Cervelt claim.
cervelt.labeling: Cervelt is a trade name, not a generic fiber name. Deer is not among the specialty fibers of the US Wool Products Labeling Act, so under 16 CFR 303.6 the content would be disclosed with the animal's name and the word hair, fiber or blend when present at 5% or more, for example deer hair, or as fur fiber. In the EU, deer hair falls in the animal hair category of Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, and the trade name cannot replace that disclosure.
cervelt.past: Commercial history for the Cervelt name, including dates, companies and volumes, could not be verified, so none is given. The scientific record is clearer. Work on red deer photoperiod, melatonin and prolactin in the 1990s explained the timing of winter coat growth, and the 2010 ultrastructural study from AgResearch showed that red deer underhair is structurally close to fine wool. That is the kind of evidence a producer would need to support textile use, but it does not describe any specific commercial product.
facts: advanced about 35 days by melatonin; delayed about 20 days by lactation with restricted food

abaca.origin: Abaca is Musa textilis, a banana relative indigenous to the Philippines whose fiber is traded as Manila hemp even though it is unrelated to Cannabis. Philippine agencies report that the country supplies roughly 85 to 87 percent of world abaca fiber, with Ecuador supplying most of the remainder and Costa Rica a small share. Production is concentrated in smallholder farms in regions such as Bicol, Eastern Visayas and Mindanao, and a large part of the crop is pulped rather than spun.
abaca.structure: The commercial fiber comes from vascular fiber bundles in the overlapping leaf sheaths (petiole bases) that form the pseudostem. Bundles are composites of elementary cellulose cells cemented by hemicellulose and lignin, each cell with a central lumen. Reported composition is roughly 56 to 68 percent cellulose, about 20 to 25 percent hemicellulose and 7 to 15 percent lignin, a low lignin share compared with coir. Extracted strands are typically about 1 to 3 meters long. Their porous, irregular cross-sections mean that published bundle strengths vary widely with how cross-sectional area is measured, a point stressed in fiber-testing studies.
abaca.process: At harvest the pseudostem is felled and separated into sheaths. In tuxying, an incision is made near the butt of each sheath with a tuxying knife and the outer fibrous layer (the tuxy) is pulled away in strips. Fiber is then freed from pulp by stripping: hand stripping draws the tuxy under a knife pressed against a wooden block, while spindle or machine stripping pulls it through a semi-mechanized stripper. Knife serration strongly affects cleanliness and grade. Separate decortication lines crush and scrape whole sheaths. Fiber is sun dried, graded and baled, then routed to cordage, specialty pulp or handloom weaving.
abaca.performance: Abaca is a stiff, low-extension fiber: single-fiber tests typically record elongation at break of only about 2 to 4 percent, and bundle tensile strength values reported in the literature range from about 400 to roughly 1,000 MPa depending on method. Its lignin and cellulose balance gives useful resistance to microbial attack and to prolonged saltwater exposure, the basis of its marine cordage and fishing-net use. Alkali treatment (for example 5 percent NaOH) can raise strength for composite use but over-treatment breaks bundles into elementary fibers. Like other bast and leaf fibers it takes direct and reactive dyes and degrades under prolonged UV.
abaca.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done with care: abaca behaves like other cellulosics, burning readily with a paper-like smell and leaving light gray ash. Under the microscope it shows long, stiff bundles of lumened cells rather than the convoluted ribbons of cotton. FTIR confirms a cellulose and lignin spectrum but does not distinguish abaca from other Musa leaf fibers, so products described as banana fiber and abaca can be confused. Grade identity follows Philippine standards, and visual grading is considered reliable mainly for hand-stripped fiber.
abaca.labeling: In the Philippines, grading follows Philippine National Standards PNS/BAFS 180:2016 (hand-stripped and spindle or machine-stripped fiber) and PNS/BAFS 181:2016 (decorticated fiber), administered with the Philippine Fiber Industry Development Authority. Top grades such as S2 and S3 are the whitest and cleanest, used for specialty paper, while darker grades go to cordage and packaging. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists abaca as a permitted fibre name (Annex I). In the US, textile products covered by the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.; 16 CFR Part 303) disclose natural fibers by common name, and calling abaca simply hemp would be misleading.
abaca.past: Abaca cordage from the Philippines became an important nineteenth-century export for ship rigging, bought largely from smallholders by merchant houses. Under American rule after 1898 the trade expanded further, and from about 1903 to 1904 contract laborers from Japan began working abaca around Davao; the Ohta Development Company, founded in 1907, organized a Japanese-run plantation economy there, and by the late 1930s Davao had a Japanese community of roughly 20,000 people. Later demand shifted toward pulp: Japan's National Printing Bureau states that its banknote paper uses mitsumata and abaca pulp, and abaca is also used in tea bags and filters. Abaca bunchy top disease has since devastated plantations in Leyte and Samar.
